newsitem.title: USA: New Mobil pump technology already challenged.
newsitem.headline: New Mobil pump technology already challenged.

text.p: Mobil Corp, the second leading U.S. gasoline marketer, will be introducing a new gasoline pump technology next month, but Royal Dutch/Shell Group's Shell Oil Co, the Number One seller, is already testing the next pump innovation -- robotics.

Mobil is now installing its Speedpass pay-at-the-pump system, using Texas Instruments Inc technology, in nine markets across the country and will introduce it to the public starting May 1, spokeswoman Jeanne Mitchell told Reuters.
She said the nine are the Boston area, including nearby Rhode Island and New Hampshire; Washington, D.C.; Tampa; Miami; Orlando, Fla.; Chicago; Detroit; Los Angeles; and San Diego.

Customers using Speedpass will be able to purchase gasoline by waving miniature electonic devices attached to their key chains in front of designated gasoline pumps. No credit cards or cash will be required to complete purchases, Mobil said when it announced plans to take the program natiowide.
But the Texas Instruments technology Mobil is using has gained full acceptance so far with only one gasoline pump maker, Dresser Industries Inc's Wayne Division.

Rival pump maker Gilbarco Inc is is installing the Texas Instruments technology on its pumps in service at Mobil stations, Mitchell said. But Gilbarco product development manager Craig Hartsell told Reuters Gilbarco is "optimistic that Micron (Technology Inc's Microstamp) will become the industry standard."
Ultimately an open architecture and an industry pay-at-the-pump standard will be developed, he said Friday.
The General Electric Co Plc subsidiary is working with Shell's Shell Oil Products Co to develop Easy Pay, which will be introduced in two test markets this summer.
That is about one year behind Mobil's testing, which began in St. Louis last August.

Gilbarco is "working with a number of other oil companies" on use of the Micron technology used in Easy Pay, Hartsell said. He declined to name the others, but projected "six months from now most of the majors" will announce systems.

In response to a question about reports Amoco Corp would soon start testing a similar system, Amoco spokesman Neil Geary said the company has "a number of concepts in test right now, (but is) very pleased with the way pay-at-the-pump is going now." Chicago-based Amoco is not planning a Chicago test, he said.
Last week, a third major pump maker -- Tokheim Corp -- said it was developing pumps using the Micron technology.
But Shell and Gilbarco have also begun field testing the robotic Smart Pump in Sacramento, Calif., Shell said.

It said the automated Smart Pump fueling system will change the way motorists fuel their vehicles by using advanced robotic technology to dispense fuel -- without the customer ever getting out of the car.

The customer will pull up and from the car select the grade of fuel and payment method. The Smart Pump will identify the make and model of the car and then position its robotic arm to automatically open the fuel door and dispense fuel through a special cap available from Shell.
The typical fueling process for the average vehicle will take about two minutes, Shell said.

Besides Gilbarco, Shell said it is working with International Submarine Engineering Ltd, Textron Inc's HR Textron and Stant Corp on the Smart Pump technology. Stant agreed to be acquired by Tomkins Plc earlier this week.
